sentences: Every time you buy something online, your browser shares a secret with a computer it has never met, over a network anyone can listen to.
How is that even possible?
The answer is RSA.
Classic encryption uses one shared key.
The same key locks and unlocks the message.
That works great, if you already share the key.
But how do you send the key itself, when anyone can read what you send?
For centuries, this was the unsolved problem of cryptography.
In nineteen seventy-seven, Rivest, Shamir and Adleman published a different idea: use two keys.
A public key, which you hand out to everyone, and a private key, which you never share.
Think of the public key as an open padlock.
Anyone can snap it shut, but only the private key can open it.
To build such a lock, RSA uses a mathematical trapdoor.
Multiplying two large prime numbers is easy.
But taking the result and finding the original primes is incredibly hard.
Easy in one direction, practically impossible in the other, unless you know the secret.
Let's build a tiny key pair.
Pick two primes: p equals five, and q equals eleven.
Multiply them to get n, fifty-five.
Next, compute phi of n: p minus one, times q minus one, which is forty.
Choose a public exponent e that shares no factors with forty.
We'll use three.
Finally, find d, so that e times d leaves a remainder of one when divided by forty.
That's twenty-seven, because eighty-one is two forties plus one.
The public key is e and n.
The private key is d.
Everything else gets thrown away.
Now Alice wants to send the number seven.
She uses Bob's public key: seven to the power of three is three hundred forty-three.
Modulo fifty-five, that leaves thirteen.
She sends thirteen.
Bob raises thirteen to the power of twenty-seven, modulo fifty-five, and gets back exactly seven.
The eavesdropper only ever saw thirteen.
Why does this work?
Because e and d were chosen as inverses, raising to e and then to d is the same as raising to e times d, which brings every message back to itself.
To find d, an attacker needs phi of n, and to get phi, they need to factor n.
That's the trapdoor.
RSA also works in reverse.
If Bob encrypts something with his private key, anyone can check it with his public key.
Only Bob could have produced it.
That's a digital signature, and it's how your browser knows a website is really who it claims to be.
Real RSA keys don't use five and eleven.
They use primes hundreds of digits long, giving keys of two thousand forty-eight bits or more.
And in practice, RSA is used to exchange or sign a small secret, while faster algorithms encrypt the actual data.
So, to recap.
Two keys: one public, one private.
Security rests on how hard it is to factor a huge number.
And that simple idea protects almost everything you do online.
